analysis.one_liner: Lets taxpayers deduct unlimited investment losses against their regular income.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or any further action.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, if you sell an investment at a loss, you can subtract that loss from your taxes only up to a small annual limit, with the rest carried to future years; corporations cannot deduct capital losses at all. This bill would wipe out those limits entirely, letting investors and corporations subtract every dollar of investment losses from the income they owe tax on. It was introduced by Rep. Robert Dornan with 8 Republican cosponsors and never moved past the House Ways and Means Committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Investors and corporations with large investment losses, who could deduct the full amount against wages, business income, or other taxable income instead of the current small annual cap, drastically cutting their tax bills in years when their investments lose money.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the provisions of the tax code that cap capital loss deductions, including the section that limits losses to a small amount against ordinary income and the sections that deny corporations capital loss deductions entirely [S3].
The CRS summary describes the bill as repealing limitations on the deductibility of capital losses [S2].
The repeal would apply to tax years beginning after December 31, 1993, with a transition rule carrying over one year of previously limited losses [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers generally: every dollar of investment loss that a high-income investor or corporation deducts is a dollar the Treasury does not collect, which either widens the deficit or shifts the tax burden onto wages and ordinary income.

drawbacks.text: Unlimited loss deductibility would let investors use losses on speculative bets to erase tax owed on wages and other ordinary income, a benefit worth the most to people with the largest portfolios, and the bill contained no revenue offset [S3].
Removing the corporate bar on capital loss deductions would allow corporations to deduct investment losses with no cap, reducing corporate tax collections [S3].
An honest supporter would acknowledge that the current cap exists partly to prevent tax-driven loss harvesting; this bill would remove that guardrail without replacing the revenue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers a straightforward tax cut, but nearly all of it flows to investors and corporations with large losses, which skews heavily toward the wealthy; the cost is forgone federal revenue borne by everyone else. The current limits also protect against tax games that convert ordinary income into tax-free outcomes. It is a narrow benefit with a broad cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and sat there until the Congress ended, with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Dornan introduced the bill on January 27, 1993, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the bill never left committee before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].
The bill had 8 cosponsors, all Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, the current cap on capital loss deductions stayed in place, preserving federal revenue and keeping the tax burden off wage earners; investors with large losses did not get the deduction. Short:

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Ordinary taxpayers kept the current revenue base

for.name: Rep. Robert K. Dornan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal capital loss deduction limits.

for.name: 8 Republican House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none took further action on the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Ways and Means
against.role: Committee of referral (Chair: Dan Rostenkowski, D-IL)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no action; the bill never received a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Republicans, but no member or group publicly opposed the bill; it simply never advanced, so no recorded partisan vote exists.

industries.industry: Investors and investment funds with capital losses
industries.note: Unlimited deductibility would let large investors erase tax on wages and business income with investment losses, a benefit worth the most to the biggest portfolios. The cost is forgone Treasury revenue spread across other taxpayers.
The bill repeals the provision that bars corporations from deducting capital losses, letting them write off investment losses with no cap. Any revenue loss is borne by other taxpayers.
